name: London
info: London is the capital of England and the United Kingdom, on the River Thames in south-east England, founded by the Romans as Londinium about 47 CE and since a major port, seat of government and commercial centre.

facts.founded: By the Romans as Londinium, about 47 CE, some four years after their invasion of 43 CE; no Iron Age town has been found on the site
facts.where: On the River Thames in south-east England, at the river's lowest bridging point, in England, United Kingdom
facts.known: The Roman wall and Londinium; the Tower of London; Westminster Abbey and the Palace of Westminster; the Great Fire of 1666; St Paul's Cathedral; London Bridge; the East India Company; the Blitz
facts.today: The capital of England and the United Kingdom, a metropolis around the historic City of London.

t: London was founded by the Romans about 47 CE and was destroyed by Boudica's Iceni within about fifteen years, then rebuilt as a planned town.
After a post-Roman decline it revived inside its old walls from 886, and from 1066 it was the place where England's kings were crowned and where government settled at Westminster.
Plague in 1665 and 1666 and the Great Fire of 1666 struck the old city, and from the 19th century it grew into the world's largest city, with 6.7 million people in 1900.
dyk: In 1666 the Great Fire destroyed about 60 per cent of London, including 87 parish churches, yet it is believed to have cost at most 16 lives.
ev: The Romans found Londinium, about four years after their invasion

sections.origins:
London stands on the River Thames in south-east England, at what is described as the river's lowest bridging point. The Thames was once much broader and shallower, with extensive wetlands, and at high tide its shores reached five times their present width. Archaeologists have found traces of earlier activity on the south foreshore, where the now underground River Effra flows into the river: a large timber structure dated to between 4800 and 4500 BCE, and the remains of a Bronze Age bridge whose timbers were dated to between 1750 and 1285 BCE. Struck flint at the Fulham Palace site shows prehistoric activity from the late Mesolithic and early Neolithic, and activity there ends in the late Iron Age, around 300 BCE.

No Iron Age town has been found. The archaeologist Leslie Wallace is quoted as saying that, because no late pre-Roman Iron Age settlements or significant domestic refuse have been found despite extensive excavation, arguments for a purely Roman foundation of London are now common and uncontroversial. Scattered Brythonic settlements existed in the area, and the name London came into Latin, Old English and Welsh from Common Brythonic, probably from a lost Celtic form *Londonjon.

The Romans founded Londinium as a civilian town about four years after their invasion of 43 CE, around 47 CE. In 60 or 61 CE the Iceni, led by their queen Boudica, stormed the town and burnt it down. It was rebuilt as a planned Roman town and recovered after perhaps ten years.
sections.growth:
Roman Londinium grew rapidly after its rebuilding. By its height in the 2nd century it had a population of around 60,000 and major public buildings: the largest basilica north of the Alps, temples, bath houses, an amphitheatre and a large fort for the garrison. Political instability and recession from the 3rd century led to a slow decline, and by the end of the 5th century the Roman city was practically abandoned.

The Anglo-Saxon settlement of Lundenwic, a trading settlement outside the walls along what is now the Strand, grew to a likely population of 10,000 to 12,000. By about 680 it was a major port again. After 886 life and trade moved back inside the old walls, and London grew slowly until a dramatic increase around 950. In the 11th century it was the largest town in England. The population was somewhat more than 15,000 in 1100 and roughly 80,000 in 1300 by one estimate, and some 18,000 and nearly 100,000 by another.

In the 16th and 17th centuries trade expanded to Russia, the Levant and the Americas, and monopoly companies such as the Muscovy Company (1555) and the East India Company (1600) were chartered in London. The population rose from an estimated 50,000 in 1530 to about 225,000 in 1605. In 1700 London handled 80 per cent of England's imports, 69 per cent of its exports and 86 per cent of its re-exports. It grew from 1 million people in 1800 to 6.7 million a century later, and its population reached a peak of 8.6 million in 1939.
sections.rulers:
Roman London formed part of the province of Britannia until the end of Roman rule in 410. Some claim that it replaced Colchester as the capital in the 2nd century, though no surviving evidence shows it was ever the capital, and it is also said to have superseded Colchester as principal city in 100. Anglo-Saxon London belonged first to the Middle Saxons, was part of the kingdom of the East Saxons by the early 7th century, and came under direct Mercian control in the 730s.

Viking raiders sacked the city in 842 and 851, and the Danish Great Heathen Army wintered there in 871. The city stayed in Danish hands until 886, when forces of Alfred the Great of Wessex captured it and placed it under Ealdorman Æthelred of Mercia. After Æthelred died in 911 it passed to Wessex. London resisted Sweyn Forkbeard in 994 and was the last place to hold out in 1013 before it too submitted. Cnut besieged it in 1016, and after the Battle of Assandun Edmund Ironside ceded England north of the Thames to him.

After 1066 William of Normandy was crowned at Westminster Abbey and built the Tower of London. Government settled at Westminster from the 12th century, while the City of London kept its own administration under the Corporation. The Greater London Council replaced the old County of London in 1965, was abolished in 1986, and the Greater London Authority was created in 2000.
sections.life:
Londinium was ethnically diverse, with inhabitants from Britannia, continental Europe, the Middle East and North Africa. Six of the traditional seven city gates, Ludgate, Newgate, Aldersgate, Cripplegate, Bishopsgate and Aldgate, are of Roman origin; Moorgate is medieval. The Roman wall, built between 180 and 225, was about 3 kilometres long, 6 metres high and 2.5 metres thick, and defined the City's perimeter for centuries.

Mellitus, the first post-Roman bishop, arrived in 604 after King Sæberht of Essex converted, and founded the first St Paul's Cathedral. The first Jews arrived about 1070. They suffered violence in 1190, a punitive levy in 1224 and 500 deaths in 1264, and were expelled by Edward I in 1290. Medieval trade was organised in craft guilds, which effectively controlled the city and elected the Lord Mayor, and before the Reformation more than half the area of London belonged to religious houses. Foreigners made up an estimated 4,000 of 100,000 residents by 1600, and met xenophobia that increased after the 1580s.

In the 17th century the nave of Old St Paul's was the daytime meeting place of Londoners, with merchants conducting business in its aisles. St Paul's Churchyard was the centre of the book trade. Shakespeare built the Globe Theatre in Southwark in 1599. Coffeehouses were places of debate in the 18th century, and Fleet Street became the centre of the press. Irish refugees of the Great Famine settled in the Victorian city, and at one point Catholic Irish made up about 20 per cent of the population.
sections.crises:
Medieval London was made of narrow, twisting streets and combustible timber and straw, and fire was a constant threat. A tornado struck on 17 October 1091, reportedly destroying over 600 houses and killing two people. During the Peasants' Revolt of 1381 rebels led by Wat Tyler entered the city, stormed the Tower and executed the Lord Chancellor, Archbishop Simon Sudbury; Tyler was stabbed to death by the Lord Mayor William Walworth at Smithfield. The Black Death in the mid-14th century killed between nearly a third and at least half of the population, by different estimates.

The Great Plague of 1665 and 1666 killed between around 60,000 people, one fifth of the population, and some 100,000, by different estimates. Samuel Pepys wrote on 4 September 1665 that over 7,400 had died in one week. The Great Fire began on 2 September 1666 in a bakery in Pudding Lane and burned until Thursday. It destroyed about 60 per cent of the city, including Old St Paul's, 87 parish churches and 44 livery company halls, and at most 16 lives are believed lost.

Cholera killed 14,000 in 1848 and 6,000 in 1866. The Great Stink of 1858 preceded Joseph Bazalgette's sewers. The Gordon Riots of 1780 left 285 rioters dead. In the First World War German airships killed around 700 people. The Blitz ran from 7 September 1940 to 10 May 1941, with 71 raids and over 18,000 tonnes of high explosive, and the Second World War bombing killed about 30,000 Londoners. The Great Smog of 1952 killed between 10,000 and 12,000 by modern estimates.
sections.legacy:
After the Great Fire Christopher Wren rebuilt the ruined parish churches and designed the new St Paul's Cathedral, with its dome, which was the city's primary symbol for at least a century and a half. His plan for a new street layout was not carried out, and the rebuilt City generally followed the old street plan. The Monument commemorates the fire. The cathedral was completed in 1708 or 1710, by different reckonings.

Westminster Abbey, founded by Edward the Confessor, and the Palace of Westminster, which grew from Westminster Hall begun in 1097, remain the setting of royal ceremony and Parliament. The Tower of London, begun by William, is one of four World Heritage Sites in the city, with Kew Gardens, the Westminster site and Greenwich, where the Royal Observatory defines the prime meridian. The Roman wall still marks the line of the City's boundaries.

Bazalgette's sewers, more than 2,100 kilometres of tunnels and pipes, are still in use. The Great Exhibition of 1851 drew 6 million visitors. London was the world's largest city from about 1831 to 1925, and from the 1940s it became home to many immigrants, primarily from Commonwealth countries such as Jamaica, India, Bangladesh and Pakistan. Today it is the capital of England and the United Kingdom, with about nine million people.

summary: London was founded by the Romans as Londinium about 47 CE on the Thames. It survived destruction by Boudica, Viking attack, plague, fire and bombing, became the seat of English government at Westminster, and grew into the world's largest city in the 19th century.
